steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our dataset distillation paper. Explain what data distillation is and why it matters, argue that IPC hides storage and training-time costs of current methods, introduce our distributional distillation approach and federated subtask distillation scheme, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Data distillation: definition and motivation
2. Current methods: prototypes, latent-space distillation, IPC, scaling
3. The incomplete story: storage costs and training time beyond IPC
4. Our approach: Distributional Dataset Distillation (D3)
5. Scaling via federated distillation on subtasks
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Data distillation
- large datasets (ImageNet): image classification, single-object localization, generative tasks
- only one task needed -> synthesize relevant information only, achieve compression?
- goal (first introduced in earlier work): ‘condense’ dataset into smaller synthetic counterpart, comparable performance
- implications: storage efficiency, faster training, democratization of large-scale training
- downstream: neural architecture search, approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, knowledge distillation (data-hungry)
- continual learning, differential privacy (beats bespoke DP generators), private medical data sharing

2. Current methods
- synthetic prototypes: small subset of learnt (input, label) pairs, most ‘salient’ aspects
- often in input (image) space; recent work: latent space + decoder back to image space
- success measured by Images (or Prototypes) Per Class (IPC), limited loss of performance
- scaling: ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-21K
- SRe 2 L: \sim\!\!100\times IPC reduction on ImageNet-1K, \sim\!\!77\% accuracy recovered

3. Incomplete story
- total storage + runtime to train new models on distilled data -> efficacy much more subdued
- other artifacts: soft labels (multiple per prototype), augmentation parameters; footprint rarely reported
- distilled labels crucial (Figure 7), storage not captured by IPC (Table 7, Appendix A.1)
- true compression rate much lower than IPC implies (Figure 1, left)
- decoding/generation/augmentation -> extra post-distillation training time (Figure 1, right)
- IPC incomplete; revisit methods with comprehensive metrics

4. D3
- compression in storage size and downstream training time, not cardinality
- latent space: inter-class mutual information shared in decoder parameters; finer control (latent codes per class, latent dimensions, decoder size)
- distributional: synthetic probability distribution sampled for training data
- efficient, little extra computation downstream

5. Federated distillation
- scale to ImageNet-1K; parallelize distillation (Figure 2)
- split full classification task into subtasks (subsets of classes); local experts
- aggregate locally distilled data; generalizes to full task
- SOTA on ImageNet-1K by storage cost

6. Contributions
- high storage / training time of prototype methods, not captured by IPC
- distribution-based framework, smaller footprint; matches or beats SOTA (TinyImageNet, ImageNet-1K)
- federated distillation strategy, general applicability
- new evaluation protocols and metrics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large datasets like ImageNet can be used for many purposes, from image classification and single-object localization to generative tasks. If we only need to do one of these tasks, for example image classification, can we synthesize only the relevant information in the data and so achieve compression? Data distillation, first introduced in earlier work, tries to answer this question: how to ‘condense’ a dataset into a smaller (synthetic) counterpart, so that training on the distilled dataset gives performance comparable to training on the original dataset. Since then, this problem has received a lot of attention because of its obvious implications for data storage efficiency, faster model training, and democratization of large-scale model training. It could also speed up downstream applications like neural architecture search, approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, and knowledge distillation, which all often need data-hungry methods. Data distillation has also become a promising approach for continual learning and differential privacy, where it often does better than bespoke differentially-private data generators in both performance and privacy, and it allows private medical data sharing.

Most current state-of-the-art data distillation methods produce synthetic prototypes: a small subset of learnt (input, label) pairs that capture the most ‘salient’ aspects of the original dataset (in terms of their impact on classifier performance). These prototypes are often defined in the original input (e.g., image) space. Recently, some work propose to distill images into a latent space and use a decoder to map latent codes back to the input (image) space. Overall, dataset distillation methods have been very successful in producing much smaller datasets, usually measured in Images (or Prototypes) Per Class (IPC), with limited loss of downstream model performance. Early methods had limited scalability, but recent ones have scaled to large datasets like ImageNet-1K or even ImageNet-21K. For example, SRe 2 L achieved a \sim\!\!100\times IPC reduction on ImageNet-1K and recovered \sim\!\!77\% of the classification accuracy.

These results are encouraging, but we will show that they do not tell the whole story. If we consider the total storage (e.g., disk space used to store all the necessary distillation outputs) and the runtime needed to train new models on the distilled data, these methods look much less effective. Besides the prototypes, some of these methods output other artifacts that are needed for downstream use but whose memory footprint is rarely reported. These include soft labels (often several per prototype) and the augmentation parameters used. Distilled labels are crucial (see Figure 7) but they have a storage cost that IPC does not capture (Table 7, Appendix A.1). When we take the storage cost of these artifacts into account, the true compression rate of these methods is much lower than the IPC metric suggests (Figure 1, left). Also, decoding/generation/augmentation procedures often add post-distillation training time (Figure 1, right). Because of these observations, we argue that IPC is an incomplete metric for distillation, and that the methods developed to optimize it should be looked at again with a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics.

4. D3
- compression in storage size and downstream training time, not cardinality
- latent space: inter-class mutual information shared in decoder parameters; finer control (latent codes per class, latent dimensions, decoder size)
- distributional: synthetic probability distribution sampled for training data
- efficient, little extra computation downstream

5. Federated distillation
- scale to ImageNet-1K; parallelize distillation (Figure 2)
- split full classification task into subtasks (subsets of classes); local experts
- aggregate locally distilled data; generalizes to full task
- SOTA on ImageNet-1K by storage cost

6. Contributions
- high storage / training time of prototype methods, not captured by IPC
- distribution-based framework, smaller footprint; matches or beats SOTA (TinyImageNet, ImageNet-1K)
- federated distillation strategy, general applicability
- new evaluation protocols and metrics

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large datasets like ImageNet can be used for many purposes, from image classification and single-object localization to generative tasks. If we only need to do one of these tasks, for example image classification, can we synthesize only the relevant information in the data and so achieve compression? Data distillation, first introduced in earlier work, tries to answer this question: how to ‘condense’ a dataset into a smaller (synthetic) counterpart, so that training on the distilled dataset gives performance comparable to training on the original dataset. Since then, this problem has received a lot of attention because of its obvious implications for data storage efficiency, faster model training, and democratization of large-scale model training. It could also speed up downstream applications like neural architecture search, approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, and knowledge distillation, which all often need data-hungry methods. Data distillation has also become a promising approach for continual learning and differential privacy, where it often does better than bespoke differentially-private data generators in both performance and privacy, and it allows private medical data sharing.

Most current state-of-the-art data distillation methods produce synthetic prototypes: a small subset of learnt (input, label) pairs that capture the most ‘salient’ aspects of the original dataset (in terms of their impact on classifier performance). These prototypes are often defined in the original input (e.g., image) space. Recently, some work propose to distill images into a latent space and use a decoder to map latent codes back to the input (image) space. Overall, dataset distillation methods have been very successful in producing much smaller datasets, usually measured in Images (or Prototypes) Per Class (IPC), with limited loss of downstream model performance. Early methods had limited scalability, but recent ones have scaled to large datasets like ImageNet-1K or even ImageNet-21K. For example, SRe 2 L achieved a \sim\!\!100\times IPC reduction on ImageNet-1K and recovered \sim\!\!77\% of the classification accuracy.

These results are encouraging, but we will show that they do not tell the whole story. If we consider the total storage (e.g., disk space used to store all the necessary distillation outputs) and the runtime needed to train new models on the distilled data, these methods look much less effective. Besides the prototypes, some of these methods output other artifacts that are needed for downstream use but whose memory footprint is rarely reported. These include soft labels (often several per prototype) and the augmentation parameters used. Distilled labels are crucial (see Figure 7) but they have a storage cost that IPC does not capture (Table 7, Appendix A.1). When we take the storage cost of these artifacts into account, the true compression rate of these methods is much lower than the IPC metric suggests (Figure 1, left). Also, decoding/generation/augmentation procedures often add post-distillation training time (Figure 1, right). Because of these observations, we argue that IPC is an incomplete metric for distillation, and that the methods developed to optimize it should be looked at again with a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics.

To address this, we propose a new dataset distillation method with efficient compression, not in terms of dataset cardinality (i.e., IPC), but directly in terms of storage size and downstream model training time. Distilling into the latent space allows a more compact representation of the data, because inter-class mutual information is shared in the decoder parameters, and it also gives finer-grained control on compression than working with prototypes directly (e.g., by changing the number of latent codes per class, the latent dimensions and the decoder size). We challenge the usual approach of distilling into a finite set of (latent) prototypes and instead cast the problem as a distributional one: finding a synthetic probability distribution that can be sampled to produce training data for downstream tasks. This Distributional Dataset Distillation (D3) approach gives an efficient representation of distilled data without much additional computation cost on downstream tasks.

To scale our method to large datasets like ImageNet-1K efficiently, we propose a simple but effective federated distillation scheme that parallelizes the distillation process (Figure 2). Instead of distilling the whole dataset directly, we divide the full classification task into subtasks, where each one only classifies a subset of all the classes. Data distillation is done on the subtasks, using local experts trained on the subtasks. Then we aggregate the locally distilled datasets to form the distilled data for the full task. We show that data distilled on subtasks generalizes well to the full task, which is why our federated distillation process performs well. With the distributional representation and federated distillation, we get SOTA performance on ImageNet-1K as measured by storage cost.

Our contributions are:

- • We show that state-of-the-art prototype-based data distillation methods have unexpectedly high storage costs and post-distillation training times. This is under-reported and not captured by commonly-used compression metrics (e.g., IPC, the number of distilled items per class). The large storage cost and training time could make these methods less usable in practice.

- • We propose a new distillation framework with a smaller memory footprint that distills datasets into distributions. It extends recent methods that distill into a latent space so that they work on (latent) distributions. We show that this method matches or beats state-of-the-art distillation methods in prediction accuracy on several datasets (e.g., TinyImageNet, ImageNet-1K), with smaller storage costs.

- • We propose a simple but effective federated distillation strategy that lets the distillation training process be parallelized, and that can be applied more generally than just to our method.

- • Based on the observations above, we propose new evaluation protocols and metrics for dataset distillation methods that better characterize the extent of ‘distillation’, and we compare existing work and our work along these axes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large datasets such as ImageNet [1] can be used for a variety of purposes, ranging from image classification and single-object localization to generative tasks. If one only needs to accomplish one of those tasks, say image classification, can we synthesize only the relevant information in the data and thus achieve compression? The goal of data distillation, first introduced by [2], is to answer this question: how to ‘condense’ a dataset into a smaller (synthetic) counterpart such that training on the distilled dataset achieves performance comparable to training on the original dataset. Since its inception, this problem has attracted significant attention due to its obvious implications for data storage efficiency, faster model training, and the democratization of large-scale model training. It also promises to speed up downstream applications such as neural architecture search, approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, and knowledge distillation, all of which often require data-hungry methods [3]. Moreover, data distillation has emerged as a promising approach for continual learning [4] and differential privacy [5], often outperforming bespoke differentially-private data generators in terms of both performance and privacy, and allowing for private medical data sharing [6].

Most current state-of-the-art data distillation methods produce synthetic prototypes: a small subset of learnt (input, label) pairs that capture the most ‘salient’ (in terms of their impact on classifier performance) aspects of the original dataset. These prototypes are often defined in the original input (e.g., image) space ([2,7]). Recently, some work [8,9,10] proposes to distill images into a latent space and use a decoder to map latent codes back to the input (image) space. Overall, dataset distillation methods have achieved remarkable success in producing much smaller datasets, typically measured in Images (or Prototypes) Per Class (IPC), with limited loss of downstream model performance. While early methods had limited scalability, recent ones scale to large datasets like ImageNet-1K or even ImageNet-21K [11,12,13]. For example, SRe 2 L [14] achieved a \sim\!\!100\times IPC reduction on ImageNet-1K while recovering \sim\!\!77\% of the classification accuracy.

Although encouraging, these results tell an incomplete story, as we will show. When considering the total storage (e.g., disk space used to store all necessary distillation outputs) and the runtime needed to train new models on the distilled data, the efficacy of these methods is much more subdued. Beyond the prototypes, some of these methods output other artifacts that are necessary for downstream use but whose memory footprint is rarely reported. These include soft labels (often multiple per prototype) and the augmentation parameters used [15,11,12]. Distilled labels are crucial (see Figure 7) but incur a storage cost that is not captured by IPC (Table 7, Appendix A.1). Once the storage cost of these artifacts is taken into account, the true compression rate of such methods is much lower than the IPC metric implies (Figure 1, left). On the other hand, decoding/generation/augmentation procedures often translate into additional post-distillation training time (Figure 1, right). In light of these observations, we argue that IPC is an incomplete metric of distillation, and that the methods developed to optimize it should be revisited with a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics.

In response, we propose a new dataset distillation method with efficient compression properties, not in terms of dataset cardinality (i.e., IPC), but directly in terms of storage size and downstream model training time. Distilling into the latent space not only allows a more compact representation of the data by sharing inter-class mutual information in decoder parameters, but also offers finer-grained control on compression than working directly with prototypes (e.g., by varying the number of latent codes per class, the latent dimensions and the decoder size). We challenge the conventional approach of distilling into a finite set of (latent) prototypes and instead cast the problem as a distributional one: finding a synthetic probability distribution that can be sampled to produce training data for downstream tasks. This Distributional Dataset Distillation (D3) approach yields an efficient representation of distilled data without incurring much additional computation cost on downstream tasks.

To scale our method efficiently to large datasets such as ImageNet-1K, we propose a simple-yet-effective federated distillation scheme that parallelizes the distillation process (Figure 2). Instead of distilling the entire dataset directly, we divide the full classification task into subtasks, each of which classifies only a subset of all classes. Data distillation is performed on the subtasks using local experts trained on them, and the locally distilled datasets are then aggregated to form the distilled data for the full task. We show that data distilled on subtasks generalizes well to the full task, which ensures the good performance of our federated distillation process. Using the distributional representation and federated distillation, we achieve SOTA performance on ImageNet-1K as measured by storage cost.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We show that state-of-the-art prototype-based data distillation methods yield unexpectedly high storage costs and post-distillation training times, an under-reported phenomenon that commonly-used compression metrics (e.g., IPC, the number of distilled items per class) do not capture. The large storage cost and training time could hinder the usability of these methods in practice.

- • We propose a novel distillation framework with a smaller memory footprint that distills datasets into distributions, extending recent methods that distill into a latent space to operate on (latent) distributions. We show that this method matches or outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods in prediction accuracy on various datasets (e.g., TinyImageNet, ImageNet-1K), with smaller storage costs.

- • We propose a simple-yet-effective federated distillation strategy that allows the distillation training process to be parallelized and that is applicable beyond our specific method.

- • In response to the observations above, we propose new evaluation protocols and metrics for dataset distillation methods that more accurately characterize the extent of ‘distillation’, and we compare existing work and ours along these axes.
